quote: Dieses scheint die richtige Verallgemeine- rung der conformen Abbildung zu sein.
english: This seems to be the correct generalisation of conformal mapping.
topic: The page gives literature references on orthogonal substitution coefficients and on functions with periodic continued fraction expansions, a remark on Cantor's table of representations of even numbers as sums of two primes with an averaging estimate, and the idea of mappings between n-dimensional regions governed by linear PDEs as a generalisation of conformal mapping.

triage.modern_statement: Hilbert's remark is a programme, not a precise statement. The idea: look at maps between domains in R^n (n ≥ 3) whose component functions satisfy a given system of linear PDEs. In the plane, the Cauchy–Riemann system is the linear system that defines conformal maps, and Hilbert suggests that maps defined this way are the 'right' generalisation of conformal mapping to n dimensions. The note does not say which PDE system is meant or what property is supposed to carry over, so there is no well-defined yes/no question to settle.
triage.answered_by: No one answered this specific remark, and I found no source that cites it. The question of what generalises conformal mapping to higher dimensions was taken up later along several lines. (a) Liouville's theorem (1850, before this note) already showed that in dimension n ≥ 3 the only conformal maps are Möbius transformations, so a straight copy of the plane theory is impossible. (b) The main later answer is the theory of quasiconformal and quasiregular maps (Reshetnyak, Gehring, Väisälä and others, 1960s onward). These maps are tied to nonlinear elliptic PDEs (A-harmonic equations and Beltrami systems), not to linear ones. (c) Clifford analysis works with monogenic functions, which solve a linear generalised Cauchy–Riemann (Dirac) system in n dimensions. Of these, (c) is closest to Hilbert's 'linear PDE' wording, but it is a function theory and not a theory of maps between domains. None of this is among Hilbert's published problems.

evidence.claim: Liouville's theorem: in dimensions n ≥ 3 the only conformal maps are Möbius transformations, so planar conformal mapping does not generalise directly.
Liouville's rigidity theorem for 1-quasiconformal maps between domains in R^n (n ≥ 3), and the Beltrami system in higher dimensions, are still studied.
Quasiregular maps in R^n are the standard higher-dimensional generalisation of analytic/conformal maps. Reshetnyak's theorem says they are open and discrete.
Quasiregular maps are linked to A-harmonic functions, solutions of nonlinear elliptic PDEs, which include Liouville-type results.
Clifford analysis studies monogenic functions, the null-solutions of a linear generalised Cauchy–Riemann operator in higher dimensions.

triage.why: The note is a one-line opinion with no specified PDE system and no precise claim, so it cannot be marked solved or open. The broader theme of generalising conformal mapping to n dimensions was shaped first by Liouville's rigidity theorem and later by quasiconformal/quasiregular theory and Clifford analysis. Those fields are still active, as the recent arXiv papers show. However, I found no source connecting Hilbert's diary remark to any of them, so whether any of them is the generalisation he meant is my own interpretation, not something the sources establish.
